appraisal_events.evidence: cette restriction apportée pour lui au droit universel de libre circulation n'était qu'une des formes de cet esclavage, de cet amour qui lui était si cher; il attendait toute la nuit, bien inutilement; une fois cette supposition forgée, il passait des semaines à se désoler... dont il finit par apprendre que c'était un oncle d'Odette mort depuis vingt ans.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator frames Swann's devotion as slavery: he forfeits ordinary freedoms because Odette forbids him a place he wants to visit, keeps himself awake all night for a message that never comes, and sustains weeks of groundless jealousy over a supposed rival who turns out to be Odette's dead uncle.

status_effects.explanation: Swann is reduced to anxious dependency, sleepless waiting on Odette's movements, and irrational jealousy that consumes his days.

The narrator's account of Swann's credulous acceptance of Odette's transparent lies, contrasted with his readiness to doubt a truthful friend, and his absurd suspicion of a dead uncle, casts him in a mildly pathetic light.

The narrator states explicitly that Odette's very indifference and forgetfulness toward Swann bind him to her more effectively than any deliberate coquetry, giving her the stronger local hold in the relationship.

ambiguities: Much of the passage renders Swann's 'esclavage' through free indirect style and his own interior reasoning rather than pure external narration; he himself calls this love 'si cher', so the diminishment is partly self-aware and even embraced rather than a straightforward external verdict, which softens (without reversing) the negative reading.
